title: Return one thing, update another
sub: LCA and the maximum path: what the recursion hands to the parent and what it records as the answer
cards/0/title: LCA: the problem and the signal
cards/0/body:
Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree (LeetCode #236). Given the root of a binary tree and two of its nodes, p and q, find their lowest common ancestor — the deepest node whose subtree contains both p and q; a node counts as a descendant of itself. There are 2 to 10⁵ nodes, values are distinct, p ≠ q, and both are in the tree. The tree is a plain one, not a BST: there is no key order.

On the tree [3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, null, null, 7, 4]: LCA(7, 8) = 3 — the paths to them split at the root; LCA(7, 4) = 2; LCA(5, 4) = 5 — p itself, because q lies below it.

The signal: the answer is about a pair of nodes, and what we know about them sits in subtrees. Each subtree can report upward what it has found, and the answer appears where two reports meet. In Unity this is the common parent of two objects in the hierarchy — say, to find which UI container holds both elements.
cards/1/title: Naive: two paths, or Contains at every level
cards/1/body:
The brute-force solution finds the path from the root to p and the path to q (a depth-first walk with a list holding the current path) and compares them from the start: the last common node is the LCA. That is O(n) time, but two passes and O(n) memory for the paths.

A worse version, written without thinking: walk down from the root and at every node ask a Contains function whether p and q are both in the left subtree, and if not, both in the right one. Each Contains walks a subtree, O(its size). On a chain of n nodes with p and q at the bottom that is n + (n − 1) + … ≈ n²/2: 5·10⁹ steps for n = 10⁵.

The repeated work is plain: the same subtree is walked again at every level. We want each subtree walked once, reporting its result upward.
cards/2/q: The Contains solution: at every node ask whether p and q are both in the left subtree (if so, go left), otherwise whether both are in the right one. The tree is a chain of 10⁵ nodes, and p and q are the bottom two. Roughly how many steps?
cards/2/options/0: ≈ 5·10⁹: at every level Contains walks almost everything below again
cards/2/explain: At depth i there are still n − i nodes below, and Contains walks them again: n + (n − 1) + … ≈ n²/2 = 5·10⁹. At about 10⁸ operations per second that is roughly a minute. A single recursion that reports its findings upward visits each node once.
cards/2/wrong/1: That is how the single-recursion solution behaves. Contains at every level walks the lower part of the tree all over again.
cards/2/wrong/2: A logarithm would appear on an even tree, where subtrees halve. On a chain the subtree shrinks by just one node per step.
cards/3/title: One recursion and a contract on the return value
cards/3/body:
Let the function for a subtree return a single value with this meaning: null — neither p nor q is in the subtree; p or q — one of them was found; their LCA — both were found.

The rules. If the node is empty or is p or q itself, return it and do not look deeper. That is correct: if the other one lies below, this node is the answer; if it is in another branch, the other side will find it. Otherwise ask the left and right subtrees. Both sides returned non-null — p and q are on different sides, this node is where they split, and it is the answer. Otherwise pass up whichever is non-null.

Invariant: the return value says what the subtree contains; once both have been found somewhere, the answer rises to the root as the only non-empty side. Each node once: O(n) time, O(h) stack.
cards/3/flow/0: null, p or q → return it
cards/4/task: Step through LCA for p = 7, q = 8 on the example tree. Badges show what each subtree returned. The rig will stop twice and ask what happens next.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Return 7: one finding is already there
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Return 3: the root is everyone’s ancestor
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: The root’s left subtree returned 7. What does the code do at the root, 3?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: So far the root only knows about 7, and one side cannot tell where the other node is. The right call LowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q) always happens. Returning 3 “just in case” is wrong: if q were 4, the answer would be 2, and it would come from the left.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: 7 came from the root’s left, 8 from its right. What does 3 return?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: Both sides are non-null: p is on the left, q on the right. No node below the root has both in its subtree, so 3 is the deepest common ancestor. If there were nodes above 3, this answer would rise through them as the only non-empty side.
cards/5/body:
Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (LeetCode #124). A path is a sequence of nodes where neighbours are joined by an edge and each node appears at most once; it need not pass through the root, but it has at least one node. Find the largest sum of values along a path. Up to 3·10⁴ nodes, values from −1000 to 1000. For [-10, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] the answer is 42: the path 15 → 20 → 7. Naively, try every pair of nodes and add up the path between them: O(n²) pairs, and each path still has to be walked.

Every path has a topmost node — where the path “turns”. The sum of such a path is the best way down to the left + the node + the best way down to the right. But the parent cannot extend this path: a path through the parent can enter the node along one branch only — two branches plus the parent is a fork, not a path.

So a node has two different quantities. It returns to its parent the downward gain val + max(left, right) — a path that can continue upward. It updates the global answer with the turning path val + left + right. A negative branch gain counts as 0: it is better not to take that branch. And best starts at int.MinValue, not 0: the path is non-empty, so if all values are negative the answer is below zero. That is this lesson’s template — return one thing, update another. O(n) time, O(h) stack.
cards/6/q: Assemble the solution: what to return and what to update.
cards/6/explain: best starts at int.MinValue: the path is non-empty, and when all values are negative the answer is below zero. A negative branch gain is cut to 0. best gets the path turning at the node, both branches at once. Only one branch goes up, the better one: the parent continues the path through it.
cards/7/task: Step through the trace on [-10, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]. Badges show what a node returned upward, best is shown below. The rig will stop twice and ask what gets recorded and what gets returned.
cards/7/goal/asks/0/q: 15 returned 15, 7 returned 7, best = 15. What does node 20 do?
cards/7/goal/asks/0/explain: The path turning at 20: 15 + 20 + 7 = 42 — a new best. But only one branch goes up: 20 + max(15, 7) = 35. Returning 42 is wrong: the parent −10 would attach itself to a path that has already forked at 20.
cards/7/goal/asks/1/q: The root −10: 9 came from the left, 35 from the right. What next?
cards/7/goal/asks/1/explain: The turn at the root: 9 − 10 + 35 = 34 < 42, the best stays. Upward goes −10 + 35 = 25, even though nobody is above: one function serves every node. The answer is best, not what the root returned: 42, not 25.
cards/8/q: On the tree [-3] this code returns 0, but the answer is −3. Tap the buggy line.
cards/8/explain: A path has at least one node, so when all values are negative the answer is the largest of them, and it is below zero. Starting with best = 0 means “an empty path with sum 0”, which the problem does not allow. Start at int.MinValue, and assign it inside MaxPathSum so a repeated call does not inherit the old best. Cutting branches to 0 in Gain is a different matter: dropping a branch is allowed, but the node itself is always on the path.
cards/9/title: The same template: diameter, balance, LCA in a BST and in a hierarchy
cards/9/body:
Diameter (#543) — the length of the longest path in edges. Return the height, update best = max(best, hl + hr): the path turning at a node has hl + hr edges. The same pair as in the maximum path, only with ones instead of values.

Is it balanced (#110: at every node the subtree heights differ by at most 1). Naively, recompute the children’s heights for every node: each node is recounted at every level above it, O(n log n) on an even tree. In one pass: return the height, and −1 as a “no longer balanced” signal that rises to the root. O(n).

LCA in a BST (#235) — the key order decides: if p and q are both smaller than the node, the LCA is on the left; both larger — on the right; otherwise it is the node itself. One walk down, no recursion, O(h).

LCA with parent links. A Transform has parent, so there is no need to walk the whole tree: compute the depths, lift the deeper node to the other’s depth, and step up together until they meet. O(depth), zero allocations.
cards/10/q: You are solving Maximum Path Sum out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/10/items/0: Clarify: a path has at least one node, need not pass through the root, values can be negative
cards/10/items/1: Naive: for every pair of nodes walk the path between them — O(n²) pairs, each walked too
cards/10/items/2: Idea: a path has a top node; return the one-way gain to the parent, record the turning path in best
cards/10/items/3: Write the code: negative branches become 0, best starts at int.MinValue
cards/10/items/4: Run [-10, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]: 20 records 42 but returns 35
cards/10/items/6: Edge cases: all values negative, a single node, a chain
cards/10/explain: Here the clarifications solve half the problem: “at least one node” and “negative values” are exactly the two traps in the code. Then the naive solution, the idea with two quantities, the code and a run that shows the recorded and returned values differ.
cards/11/title: Why it is correct, and where the stack runs out
cards/11/body:
Both solutions are post-order: a node decides after its children. Correctness follows from the meaning of the return value.

LCA. If p and q are in different subtrees of node x, no node below x contains both — so x is the lowest, and it is the first node on the way up where both sides are non-null. If q lies under p, the call for p returns p without going down, and at every ancestor the other side returns null — p rises to the root. The code relies on the condition “both are in the tree”: if q might be missing, it returns p as the answer.

Maximum path. Every path has exactly one topmost node, and there its sum is the best way down to the left + the node + the best way down to the right. best tries every top node, so it sees the best path too.

Depth. #236 has up to 10⁵ nodes; on a chain that is 10⁵ frames — already risky for a 1 MB stack. Below is a version without recursion: parents via an explicit stack, then p’s ancestors in a set.
cards/11/deep:
Nodes as keys. TreeNode does not override Equals and GetHashCode, so the dictionary and the set compare by reference — exactly what we need. The iterative version is O(n) time and memory but does not depend on the thread stack; the walk stops as soon as both nodes have a parent.

If a node may be missing (#1644, LCA of a Binary Tree II), the return value is not enough: you also need a count of found nodes, and the walk can no longer stop at p or q — the subtree must be walked to the end.

Many queries on one tree. Binary lifting: up[k][v] is the ancestor of v 2ᵏ levels up, O(n log n) preparation, O(log n) per query. For a Unity hierarchy this is usually overkill: depths are small, and climbing parent is enough.

Overflow and state. In #124 |sum| ≤ 3·10⁴ · 1000 = 3·10⁷ — int with room to spare; with values up to 10⁹ use long. The best field is object state: not thread-safe and in need of a reset. The alternative is ref int best in the recursion or an (int gain, int best) tuple as the return value: no field and no boxing.
cards/12/q: Match the problem with what the recursion returns and what it updates.
cards/12/pairs/0/1: Return the finding; the answer is where both sides are non-null
cards/12/pairs/1/1: Walk down by key order, O(h)
cards/12/pairs/2/1: Return the gain down, update the turning path
cards/12/pairs/3/1: Return the height, update hl + hr
